reference.source: Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: One of the commonest congenital urinary tract anomalies; a duplex kidney drains through two pelvicalyceal systems, either partial (the ureters unite before reaching the bladder, giving a bifid or Y-shaped ureter) or complete (two separate ureters with two bladder orifices)

The Weigert-Meyer rule states that in complete duplication the upper pole ureter inserts ectopically, inferomedial to the lower pole ureter, and tends to obstruct, often with a ureterocele, while the lower pole ureter inserts more laterally and superiorly and tends to reflux
As a result the upper moiety tends towards obstruction and dysplasia, and the lower moiety towards vesicoureteric reflux and reflux nephropathy

An ectopic upper pole ureter that inserts below the sphincter in a girl (into the vagina, urethra or vestibule) causes continuous dribbling incontinence despite otherwise normal voiding, a classic diagnostic clue

In boys the upper pole ureter cannot insert below the continence mechanism, so incontinence does not occur; instead it may drain into wolffian derivatives and present with epididymitis or a seminal vesicle cyst

Presentations include antenatal hydronephrosis, recurrent urinary tract infection, incontinence or an incidental finding, and a ureterocele may prolapse into the urethra to cause bladder outlet obstruction

Management is guided by function and symptoms and ranges from conservative observation to endoscopic ureterocele puncture, ureteric reimplantation, ureteroureterostomy or heminephrectomy of a non-functioning moiety
reference.pathophysiology: Duplication of the collecting system results from anomalous development of the ureteric bud from the mesonephric (wolffian) duct. Two separate ureteric buds induce complete duplication with two ureters and two orifices, whereas a single bud that bifurcates early produces incomplete (partial) duplication. In keeping with the Weigert-Meyer relationship, the bud destined for the upper pole is carried more caudally and medially and joins the bladder ectopically with a tendency to obstruct and to form a ureterocele, while the lower pole bud reaches the bladder earlier and more laterally with a short intramural tunnel that predisposes to reflux. Whether the ectopic upper pole ureter terminates above or below the continence mechanism determines whether continuous incontinence occurs.
additionalDifferentials: Pelviureteric junction obstruction or simple hydronephrosis
Vesicoureteric reflux in a single system
Neurogenic bladder or other functional cause of incontinence
additionalInvestigations: Renal tract ultrasound to show two pelvicalyceal systems, upper pole hydronephrosis, a dilated ureter or a ureterocele
Micturating cystourethrogram to assess reflux and demonstrate a ureterocele
MAG3 or DMSA renal scintigraphy for the differential function and drainage of each moiety
MR urography for anatomical delineation and localisation of an ectopic ureter
Urinalysis and culture to confirm and characterise urinary tract infection
redFlags: Febrile urinary tract infection, pyelonephritis or urosepsis
A prolapsing ureterocele causing bladder outlet obstruction with bilateral upper tract dilatation and renal impairment
An obstructed non-functioning upper pole moiety
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally good; many duplex systems are asymptomatic and require no intervention. Outcomes depend on preserving renal function and controlling infection and reflux, and even moieties needing surgery usually do well overall.
pitfalls: Missing a duplex system on ultrasound when only the lower pole is well visualised
Overlooking an ectopic ureter in a girl with continuous wetness despite normal voiding and mislabelling it functional incontinence
Failing to apply the Weigert-Meyer rule and attributing obstruction or reflux to the wrong moiety
Removing a moiety that retains recoverable function
Not recognising a prolapsing ureterocele as a cause of bladder outlet obstruction
